alalal-c43874-d1e104.summary: Rubric of Article 4: whether being everywhere and in every thing belongs to God from eternity.

alalal-c43874-d1e113.summary: States the fourth question: whether being everywhere and in every thing belongs to God from eternity.

alalal-c43874-d1e122.summary: First argument for eternal omnipresence: whenever the effect relates to the cause, the cause relates to the effect, perhaps prior. Since all things are said to be in God from eternity by their relation to him as cause, God should all the more be said to be everywhere and in every thing from eternity.

alalal-c43874-d1e149.summary: Second argument: if being everywhere means giving containing power to every place, and God is from eternity able to give it, he is everywhere from eternity.

alalal-c43874-d1e162.summary: Third argument: if God is in every thing by his power to conserve, and he has this power from eternity, he is in every thing from eternity.

alalal-c43874-d1e175.summary: Fourth argument: from eternity God is in every thing that exists, since he is in himself; so he is everywhere from eternity. The reply that this is equivocal is rejected, since 'every thing' has one universal sense across past, present, future and eternal things.

alalal-c43874-d1e204.summary: Sed contra: 'God is in every thing' signifies both the extent of the divine essence and the effect of conserving in being, which was not from eternity. Against those who grant 'God is everywhere from eternity' but deny 'in every thing', 'everywhere' likewise connotes an effect, the gift of containing power to place, which was not eternal either.
claims: Both 'God is in every thing' and 'God is everywhere' connote temporal effects.

alalal-c43874-d1e243.summary: Albert's solution: both propositions are false, 'God is in every thing from eternity' and 'God is everywhere from eternity', as the last arguments prove.
claims: It is false that God is everywhere or in every thing from eternity.

alalal-c43874-d1e261.summary: Reply to the first argument: things being in God and God being in things are not said in the same way. Saying things are in God does not posit their existence, but saying God is in things posits their actual existence because of the connoted effect. The principle about reciprocal relations holds of the effect as existing in itself, not as existing in its cause.
claims: God's being in things presupposes their actual existence, while things' being in God does not.
concepts: things in God vs God in things

alalal-c43874-d1e288.summary: Reply to the second and third arguments: God is said to be everywhere or in things by the act of conserving, not by the power to conserve.
claims: Omnipresence is predicated from act, not mere power.

alalal-c43874-d1e297.summary: Reply to the last argument: it is true that from eternity God is in every thing that is, since he is in himself, but it does not follow that he is in every thing from eternity. The inference commits the fallacy secundum quid ad simpliciter, since 'thing' is first restricted to eternal things and then taken absolutely.

alalal-c43874.summary: Article 4 asks whether being everywhere and in every thing belongs to God from eternity. Arguments for it appeal to the reciprocity of cause and effect, God's eternal power to give place its containing power and to conserve, and the fact that from eternity God is in all that exists, namely himself. Albert holds that both 'God is in every thing from eternity' and 'God is everywhere from eternity' are false, because both connote temporal effects: the conservation of things and the gift of containing power to place. Things are in God without being posited as existing, but God is in things only when they actually exist. Omnipresence is predicated from act, not power, and the last argument commits the fallacy secundum quid ad simpliciter.
claims: God is not everywhere or in every thing from eternity, since these predications connote temporal effects.
God's being in things presupposes their actual existence, unlike things' being in God.
Omnipresence is said of God by reason of his act of conserving, not his power.
